> From https://blog.torproject.org/announcing-arti/:
>
> In order to make the time to work on Arti, we need to devote our resources
> in that direction. We expect that in the coming years, we will spend more
> and more time programming in Rust, and less in C. Eventually, once our Rust
> implementation of Tor is a good replacement for our C implementation, we will
> stop adding new features to the C implementation, and eventually drop support
> for it entirely.

Given the statement above, I suggest to use [arti](https://arti.torproject.org/)
to implement the bridging over Tor.

I2P has Rust implementation too, called [emissary](https://eepnet.github.io/emissary/).

At a first glance, it seems that both libraries have an "embedded" mode.

Ideally, we should use the "embedded" mode as this way we reduce system calls.
In other words, the traffic should go directly from the SOCKS5 socket to the 
remote peer (that represents a Tor/I2P/Datura user) through our Rust application.

An undesirable flow for the traffic would be `TCP socket (managed by datura)
-> TCP socket (managed by arti) -> Remote peer` as this increases the number of
calls to the Linux kernel unnesesarily (because of the additional TCP socket).

I'm currently not sure if these two libraries are flexible enough for our use
case.

I also suggest to store all connections in a map (like this https://github.com/cloudflare/quiche/blob/f0c7193c3b130d766f0d6f3e75d4f2405c85d376/quiche/examples/http3-server.rs#L123), as in the future we might introduce new features that might require sorting over the list of active/idle connections. For e.x, to disconnect slow peers, to throttle peers selectively, or in an automated manner.

BTW, quiche implements the SansIO pattern.
